brief.intro: A hospital or healthcare facility is, structurally, an ordinary building — but its mechanical and electrical systems are anything but ordinary. Operating theatres and isolation rooms need precisely controlled, pressure-cascaded and HEPA-filtered air; every bed needs certified medical gases (oxygen, medical air, vacuum) piped from a central manifold; and life-safety loads (theatre lighting, ventilators, nurse call) must switch to essential/standby power within seconds of a mains failure. The programme is paced less by the structure and more by how long it takes to fit out, validate and formally certify these specialist systems before any clinical occupancy is allowed. Many hospital projects also sit on a live campus, so infection control and phased handover constrain the sequence as much as the construction logic does.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Earthworks, utility diversions, temporary access and hoarding — often around a live, operating hospital campus.

scope.name: Structure & shell
scope.desc: Foundations, frame, floor slabs and envelope, including rooftop/plant-deck structural provisions for AHUs and chillers.

scope.name: Architectural fit-out & shielded rooms
scope.desc: Partitions, ceilings, wall protection, and lead-lined shielded rooms for imaging and radiotherapy.

scope.name: HVAC & specialist air systems
scope.desc: AHUs and ductwork delivering pressure-cascade ventilation to theatres/isolation rooms, with HEPA filtration.

scope.name: Plumbing & medical gas pipeline system (MGPS)
scope.desc: Domestic water and drainage, plus oxygen/medical air/vacuum piped from a central manifold to every bedhead.

scope.name: Electrical power & essential supply
scope.desc: Normal and essential distribution, standby generators and UPS protecting critical clinical loads.

scope.name: Fire protection & life safety
scope.desc: Sprinklers, fire alarm, smoke control and compartmentation sized for a non-evacuating (defend-in-place) building.

scope.name: ELV / nurse call / BMS
scope.desc: Structured cabling, nurse-call, access control, CCTV and the building management system tying it together.

scope.name: Medical equipment interface
scope.desc: Coordinating the room and services for owner-furnished medical equipment (imaging, OR tables, sterilisers).

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & clinical handover
scope.desc: System-by-system and integrated testing, regulatory inspection, and a phased clinical handover.

glossary.plain: the medical gas pipeline system carrying oxygen, medical air and vacuum from a central manifold to each bed or outlet.
airflow control that keeps clean rooms (theatres) at higher pressure than corridors so air flows outward, and isolation rooms at negative pressure so it flows inward.
high-efficiency filters that strip out almost all airborne particles, used in theatres and isolation rooms.
a backup electrical system (generator + UPS) that must pick up life-safety and critical clinical loads within seconds of a mains failure.
a room (imaging, radiotherapy) built with lead or concrete shielding to contain radiation.
the ELV system letting patients summon staff, integrated with clinical alarms and reporting.
construction practices — barriers, negative-pressure hoarding, dust control — used to protect live clinical areas next to the works.

must_get_right: Specialist rooms (theatres, isolation, imaging) drive the programme — their MEP validation is not a normal fit-out task; plan real time for it.
Medical gas and essential power are life-safety systems — they need formal certification/commissioning before any clinical occupancy, not just a functional test.
If work is on a live hospital campus, infection control and phased handover constrain the sequence as much as the construction logic itself.
Owner-furnished medical equipment (imaging, OR tables) has its own long lead time and installation window — coordinate it into the schedule, not as furniture.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual and regulatory-inspection milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and shell run a 6-day week; MEP fit-out and specialist-room works often move to two shifts to protect the programme; commissioning and clinical validation run against the availability of inspecting authorities and clinical end-users rather than a fixed calendar. Where the works are on a live campus, an infection-control access calendar overlays the trade calendars.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs structural weather-tightness → MEP first/second fix → specialist-room fit-out (theatres, isolation, imaging) → essential power and MGPS installation & certification → HVAC pressure-cascade balance and validation → integrated systems test → regulatory inspection → phased clinical handover. The structure itself is rarely the constraint once it is weather-tight; specialist-system validation and certification own the back end.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and room-data sheets are frozen per specialist room before rough-in; authority approvals are obtained per phase gate; owner-furnished medical equipment is free-issued to a confirmed delivery window; a single mobilisation; phasing does not require decommissioning of adjacent live clinical areas beyond what is planned.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Works adjacent to a live hospital require infection-control barriers, negative-pressure hoarding and restricted hours near operating clinical areas. Specialist commissioning engineers (HVAC validation, MGPS certification, fire cause-and-effect) are scarce and shared across systems, and are a resource constraint late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: specialist-room validation failures and re-test loops, MGPS and fire cause-and-effect re-certification, and regulatory-inspection scheduling delays outside the contractor's control. Schedule contingency is held immediately before the integrated systems test and before the regulatory inspection, rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
